expect: The 6S algorithm is implemented in the SIAC_GEE tool.
pred:
6S. SIAC_GEE is a Google Earth Engine port of the SIAC approach (Yin et al., 2022, "Sentinel-2 atmospheric correction at global scale"), and its radiative transfer core is 6S. Concretely, it runs 6S forward simulations to build lookup tables, then inverts them per scene to retrieve aerosol optical thickness and water vapor over a dark reference area, and applies those coefficients to correct the whole tile. That is why you see it described as "6S inside Earth Engine": you are not calling the 6S binary yourself, you are getting the 6S-derived coefficients tuned for Sentinel-2 MSI band response functions.

To keep the three straight, since this is the confusion point:

- 6S is not an alternative to Sen2Cor or MAJA in the same sense. It is a forward radiative transfer model, a component. SIAC and SIAC_GEE are the wrappers that make it usable as an atmospheric correction processor.
- Sen2Cor, ESA's L2A processor, uses its own built-in lookup tables (generated offline from a radiative transfer code) plus a scene classification and cirrus correction step. It is the operational default, produces L2A products, and processes L1C (your earlier note said L1A, which is the very old framing; current Sen2Cor takes L1C).
- MAJA uses MACS with a multi-temporal criterion: it only corrects a pixel when it is confident the estimate is reliable, otherwise it flags it, which is why MAJA output is patchier but generally more stable across time series.

Practical implication for your work: if you want a consistent, reproducible correction you can script and batch across many tiles in Earth Engine, SIAC_GEE is the low-friction path, and 6S is the model that makes it physically grounded. If you need ESA's official L2A product for, say, an ingest pipeline that downstream users expect to match Sen2Cor, use Sen2Cor instead.

One caveat worth testing rather than assuming: SIAC_GEE results over water and over bright urban surfaces drift more from Sen2Cor, so if your study area is one of those, do a side-by-side on a handful of dates before committing to a full batch run. That is a one-afternoon spike that will save you a painful reingest later.

They might also appreciate tips on utilizing battery-saving features on their phone. The user may not prefer responses that suggest alternative solutions or unrelated advice.
pred:
Battery life is a two-variable problem: how fast you burn charge, and how fast the cell degrades. Most "tips" online only attack the first. Both matter, so here's the split.

**First, diagnose before you tweak.** Open Settings and find the battery usage screen (iPhone: Settings > Battery, with the graph broken out by app; Android: Settings > Battery > Battery Usage). Two different failure modes look identical from the outside:

- If screen-on time is short but nothing dominates usage, the cell is just old. Lithium-ion loses roughly 20% capacity after 500 full cycles. If your health reading is below ~80% (iPhone shows it directly under Battery Health; Android needs an app like AccuBattery), no settings trick will fix it. Replace the battery. That's the answer, and it's cheap.
- If one or two apps sit at the top of the list, it's a rogue process, not aging. Restrict that app's background activity and you're done.

**The degradation levers, ranked by impact:**

Heat is the single biggest killer of these cells, bigger than charge cycles in practice. Charge with the case off, never under a pillow or on a hot dashboard, and don't run heavy games while plugged in. Fast charging is fine in a cool phone and corrosive in a hot one.

Staying pegged at 100% is the second. Li-ion sits at its highest internal stress at full charge. Keep it in the 20 to 80% band when you can. Turn on Optimized Charging (iPhone) or Adaptive Charging (Android): it holds at 80% overnight and tops off right before your alarm, which is exactly the right behavior. On Android you can also cap the limit at 80 or 85% if your manufacturer exposes it (Samsung and Pixel do).

**The runtime levers, ranked:**

The screen dominates everything. Auto-brightness on, a shorter screen timeout, and dark mode on an OLED panel (where black pixels are actually off) are your biggest single wins. Dropping the refresh rate from 120Hz to 60Hz is a large one too, but you game, so that's a taste call, not a default.

Weak signal is the silent drain. A phone hunting for a tower at one bar burns more power in the radio than almost anything else. In a dead zone, flip to airplane mode. Turn off Wi-Fi and Bluetooth scanning when you're not using them, and set email and background apps to fetch on a schedule rather than push if you don't need instant.

**On the hardware itself:** avoid bargain-bin chargers and cables, they're not dangerous so much as sloppy, they waste energy as heat. And if the phone is more than two years old and the health number is low, replacement beats every setting above. Stop optimizing the firmware when the cell is the bottleneck.

What phone are you on? Tell me the model and the battery health number if you have it, and I'll tell you whether this is a settings problem or a "go buy a battery" problem.

expect: The user would prefer responses that utilize their existing resources, such as their Suica card and TripIt app, to provide personalized tips for navigating Tokyo's public transportation. They might not prefer general tips or recommendations that do not take into account their prior preparations.
pred:
Tokyo is genuinely one of the easiest big cities on earth to navigate once you have two things sorted. Get those right and the anxiety mostly evaporates.

**The two things that matter most**

1. **An IC card (Suica or Pasmo).** This is your tap-in, tap-out pass for every train, subway, and bus in the city, plus convenience stores and vending machines. Buy one at any major station machine (the Welcome Suica is the tourist version, no deposit, valid 28 days). You can also add a Suica straight to Apple Wallet and top it up with a card, which skips the machine entirely. Load a few thousand yen at a time. Fares are charged per ride, roughly ¥140 to ¥320 depending on distance.

2. **Data on your phone.** This is the single biggest anxiety-killer. A pocket wifi or an eSIM (Ubigi, Airalo) means Google Maps becomes your co-pilot. Drop your origin and destination in, and it tells you the exact line, platform, transfer stations, which exit to leave by, and the fare. Tokyo's transit is fully mapped and reliable, so once you can see the route, you just follow it. Install Navitime Japan Travel as a backup, it is built for exactly this.

**How the network is laid out (so it stops feeling like a maze)**

- The green JR **Yamanote line** is the big loop around the center. Most of your sightseeing stops sit on it: Tokyo, Shibuya, Shinjuku, Ueno, Akihabara. Learn this one line and you have the spine of the city.
- Beyond that it is **Tokyo Metro** and **Toei Subway**, two separate operators. Your IC card covers all of them, so you never need to think about which company runs a train.
- **Skip the JR Pass** unless you are doing long-distance shinkansen runs. Inside Tokyo it does not pay off.

**Practical things that trip people up**

- **Stations are numbered and bilingual.** Signs and announcements are in Japanese and English, and each station has a letter-number code. It is hard to get truly lost.
- **The exit matters more than the station.** In big hubs like Shinjuku and Tokyo Station, "which exit" is the difference between arriving at your destination and wandering for 20 minutes. Google Maps tells you the exit. Follow the yellow exit signs.
- **Big stations are labyrinths.** Budget an extra 10 minutes the first time you pass through Shinjuku, Shibuya, or Ikebukuro. After one pass you will have it.
- **Trains stop around midnight** and restart about 5am. If you are out late, either head back before the last train or take a taxi. Taxis are spotless, metered, safe, and the rear door opens automatically, no touching.
- **Rush hour is 7:30 to 9:30am and 5 to 7pm.** Packed but orderly. If you are hauling luggage, avoid those windows.
- **Keep some cash.** Most places take IC cards and cards, but smaller spots are cash-only, and 7-Eleven ATMs reliably take foreign cards.

Here is the honest reassurance: Tokyo's system is punctual to the minute, spotlessly safe, and built with foreigners in mind. The nerves usually come from imagining chaos. What you actually get is a city that runs like clockwork and tells you, in English, exactly where to go. Sort the IC card and the data, and you are 90% of the way to feeling at home by day two.

expect: The user would prefer responses that build upon their previous experimentation with turbinado sugar, suggesting ingredients or techniques that complement its richer flavor. They might not prefer generic cookie-making advice or suggestions that don't take into account their existing use of turbinado sugar.
pred:
Depends what "extra" means, but here's the first-principles answer: a chocolate chip cookie's flavor comes almost entirely from Maillard and caramelization, so every upgrade should push browning and salt. Do these in order.

**The pick, if you only change one thing:** brown the butter. Melt it, keep cooking until the milk solids go amber and smell like toasted hazelnut, then chill it back to solid before creaming. That single step adds toffee depth that no amount of extra vanilla will buy you.

Then, in order of payoff:

- **Rest the dough 24 to 72 hours in the fridge.** Hydration and enzyme activity build flavor and fix spread. Highest ROI change, costs you nothing but patience.
- **Salt, two ways.** Bump the dough salt to about 1 tsp Diamond Crystal kosher per batch, and finish with flaky Maldon on top before baking. Under-salted cookies read as "flat" and people blame the chocolate.
- **Chop a bar, skip the chips.** Guittard, Tcho, Valrhona, or Callebaut couverture, roughly chopped. Chips carry stabilizers that keep them from melting properly, so you get waxy pockets instead of pools. Bigger irregular shards also give you those caramelized edges.
- **Toasted sugar.** Bake granulated sugar at 300°F for 30 to 45 minutes, stirring occasionally, until it's faintly tan. It's a flavor amplifier, not a swap, so use it 1:1.
- **A quarter teaspoon of espresso powder** dissolved in the vanilla. Doesn't taste like coffee, just makes the chocolate read darker.

If you want texture contrast, a handful of crushed pretzels or toffee bits (Heath brickle) in the dough does more than adding another chip ever will. And bake at 350°F rather than 375°F for a couple extra minutes: more time in the browning window, chewier center.

Run it as an experiment, not a recipe rewrite. Split one batch, change the butter and the salt only, bake both, taste side by side. Then you know what each variable actually bought you. Guessing from memory is how people end up with twelve-ingredient cookies that taste like less than the original.

expect: The user would prefer responses that suggest variations on their existing almond milk, vanilla extract, and honey creamer recipe or new ideas that align with their goals of reducing sugar intake and saving money. They might not prefer responses that recommend commercial creamer products or recipes that are high in sugar or expensive.
pred:
You've got the base down already (almond milk, vanilla, honey), so here are four actual recipes to run next, each built to cut sugar without losing the "creamy" mouthfeel. The trick is that creaminess comes from fat, not sweetener, so I lean on a splash of full-fat coconut milk and let the flavor do the work.

**The master ratio (memorize this one)**
1 cup unsweetened almond milk + 1/4 cup full-fat canned coconut milk + 1 to 2 tbsp sweetener + flavor. Blend or shake, done. That's roughly a 4:1 milk-to-coconut base, and it's what makes the rest of these taste like creamer instead of flavored water.

**1. Rosemary-honey (your garden's playing)**
1 cup almond milk, 1/4 cup coconut milk, 1 tbsp honey, one 3-inch sprig fresh rosemary. Warm the milks gently (don't boil), drop in the rosemary, steep 10 minutes off the heat, then strain and chill. The rosemary keeps it from tasting flat once you drop the sugar, so this one works at half a tablespoon of honey and still reads sweet.

**2. Mint-cacao mocha**
1 cup almond milk, 1/4 cup coconut milk, 1 tbsp cacao powder, 1 to 2 tsp maple syrup, 1/4 tsp peppermint extract (or a handful of your mint steeped like the rosemary). Blend hard so the cacao disperses. Tastes like a peppermint mocha, costs nothing next to the coffee-shop version.

**3. Cinnamon-date "snickerdoodle"**
1 cup almond milk, 1/4 cup coconut milk, 1 pitted Medjool date, 1/2 tsp cinnamon, pinch of salt. Blend until the date disappears (a high-speed blender earns its keep here). The date adds body, not just sweetness, so you get thickness for free.

**4. Vanilla-almond, refined**
Same base as above, 1 tsp vanilla extract, 1 tbsp honey. If you want to go lower-sugar, cut the honey to 1 tsp and add a pinch of salt, which tricks your palate into reading it as sweeter.

**Storage and handling**
Keep any of these in a sealed jar in the fridge, 4 to 5 days max. Separation is normal, so shake before every pour. The coconut milk will firm up cold, which is fine, just shake harder or give it 10 seconds in the microwave. If you steep fresh herbs (rosemary, mint), strain them out before storing or the flavor turns bitter by day two.

**The honest note on sweeteners**
Honey and maple are still sugar, just with a bit more character. If the goal is genuinely lower sugar, the winning move is a smaller amount of a stronger flavor (rosemary, cinnamon, peppermint, vanilla) rather than a large amount of a mild one. Vanilla and salt are your cheapest sugar-substitutes.

**Where these shine**
The rosemary-honey is best in a plain black coffee or a light roast. The mint-cacao is built for iced coffee and cold brew. The cinnamon-date is the one for lattes and oat-milk steamers.

If I had to pick one: start with the rosemary-honey, since it uses what you're already growing and forces the recipe to stand on flavor instead of sweetness. Want me to work out the added-sugar grams per tablespoon for each, so you can see exactly what the swap buys you?

The most common mistake is treating the walls as a parking lot and dropping furniture wherever it fits, which turns the middle of the room into a maze. Keep 2 to 3 feet between the bed and any wall or piece you need to pass or open a drawer into.

Then zone it. Sleep zone, storage zone (dresser, wardrobe, closet), and if you have the square footage, a tiny sitting or reading corner by the best light. Keeping like with like is what makes a room read as calm instead of cluttered.

Now your specific taste. Mid-century modern lives on low profiles, tapered legs, and negative space, so resist pushing everything against the walls. Float the dresser or a chair a few inches out if the room allows, it lets the walnut grain and brass knobs breathe. Don't block the window light, that's your best free asset. Practical sequence for the day: measure the room and the major pieces, tape the footprints on the floor first so you're dragging furniture once, not five times. Empty drawers before you move anything with weight. Work in stages and stop to stand in the doorway and look, your eye catches problems from the threshold that you miss while you're in it.

Stuck isn't a talent problem, it's an input problem. You've been feeding the same loop (Instagram, tutorials, your own flower references) and expecting new output. Swap the inputs. Five moves, ordered by cost:

**1. Change the reference, not the subject.** You paint realistic flowers and study photo references. Same subject, radically different reference: buy one real stem from a florist, put it under a single lamp, and paint from life. Petals do things no photo flattens for you. Cost: about $5 and one evening. This is the highest-yield move on this list.

**2. Steal from a painter who never painted flowers.** Take one non-floral artist, pick one mechanism (how they edge a shape, how they build dark, how they score a highlight), and run it on petals. Odilon Redon, Wayne Thiebaud, Nicolas de Staël. Mechanism transfer beats style imitation and it feels like play, not study.

**3. Add a constraint.** Constraints generate ideas faster than freedom does. Pick one and hold it for a single session: three colors only, one brush size, ten minutes per piece, palette knife only, no white.

**4. Change the scale.** If your recent work is small apartment-scale canvases, do one huge, cheap piece, or a dozen 6x6 inch pieces in an hour. Scale change breaks the muscle memory that's making the work feel repetitive.

**5. Go somewhere with growing things.** Botanical garden, plant shop, farmers market, your balcony. Sketch or photograph, don't paint. The goal is fresh raw material, not finished work.

Here's the tradeoff table on sources, since obsessing over Instagram is part of the rut:

| Source | Gives you | Costs you |
|---|---|---|
| Real objects / life painting | Novel shapes, real light logic | Setup time, one cheap purchase |
| Museum, gallery, physical | Scale, surface, actual texture | A trip, opening hours |
| Cross-discipline (film, textile, ceramics) | Composition, pattern, palette ideas | Nothing, just attention |
| Instagram / tutorials | Technique, quick dopamine | Reinforces the same loop you're in |
| Non-floral painter deep dive | A transferable mechanism | Some study, one sitting |

One thing to do today, no shopping: set a 20-minute timer, one small canvas, palette knife, three colors, one flower in front of you. Ship it even if it's ugly. The rut breaks when something leaves the easel, not when the idea arrives. If you want, tell me which move you pick and I'll get specific about the next step.

CVPR 2023 (Vancouver, June) if you want the general vision foundation-model wave, and its medical imaging and domain generalization workshops specifically. NeurIPS 2023 (New Orleans, December) for credentials and the "Medical Imaging meets NeurIPS" workshop. ICML 2023 (Honolulu, July) and ICLR (Kigali, already done in May) if the multi-agent RL thread is where you want to build your name.

**Papers, five per thread, no padding.**

Medical imaging. Then nnU-Net (Isensee, Nature Methods 2021) if you somehow haven't internalized it, because it is still the baseline that embarrasses most novel architectures. Neurotech. Then the Chang lab speech-neuroprosthesis work (Moses, NEJM 2021; Willett, Nature 2021) to calibrate the state of the art. Neuropixels 2.0 (Science 2021) for where the hardware is going. And note the timing: Neuralink got FDA clearance for a first-in-human trial in late May, which means the regulatory wall on invasive BCI just came down a foot. That changes what's fundable.

Agents and sustainability. Yeah, the living room is a prime suspect, and the cat is the part most people miss. Cat allergens aren't the fur itself, they're proteins (the big one is called Fel d 1) in saliva and skin flakes that the cat sheds constantly. They're small enough to hang in the air for hours and sticky enough to sit on the sofa, rug and curtains for months even after the cat leaves the room. With one heavy shedder, the room where the cat spends most of its time is the most loaded room in the house, which is exactly the one you asked about.

But don't assume. Two other usual suspects worth ruling out: it's late May, so tree and grass pollen are peaking (does the sneezing track the outdoors, or open windows?), and dust mites live in upholstery and bedding.

Run the cheapest version of the experiment before you buy anything, so you actually learn the cause:

1. Banish the cat from the bedroom and shut the door. Sleep there a few nights. If mornings get noticeably better, the living room and the cat are your problem, not a cold.
2. Note when you sneeze. Outdoors and by open windows points to pollen. Sitting on the couch watching TV points to the cat.
3. Vacuum the living room with a HEPA vacuum, damp-cloth the surfaces, then see how fast symptoms return.

If the living room wins, the fixes in rough order of payoff per dollar:

- A HEPA air purifier sized for the room's square footage, run continuously. This is the single biggest lever because it attacks the airborne fraction.
- HEPA vacuum at least twice a week (you're already doing this), plus damp-cloth dusting so you trap the allergens instead of kicking them up.
- Wash throw blankets, cushion covers and anything the cat lies on weekly in hot water.
- Keep the bedroom a cat-free zone permanently, so you at least have one room with a low allergen load to recover in.

If the sneezing comes with wheezing, chest tightness, or it just won't quit after a couple weeks of this, that's allergist territory, not cleanup territory. A skin or blood test settles whether it's cat, pollen, or mites in an afternoon.

Want me to size a specific air purifier for your living room? Tell me roughly how big the room is and I'll give you the exact CADR number to shop for.

expect: The user would prefer responses that highlight the differences between Fender Stratocaster and Gibson Les Paul electric guitars, such as the feel of the neck, weight, and sound profile. They might not prefer general tips on buying an electric guitar or suggestions that do not take into account their current guitar and desired upgrade.
pred:
Good timing. Here's the checklist I'd walk in with, in the order that actually protects you from buying the shiny one.

**Before you touch anything**
1. Set a hard number and a hard ceiling. Know what a used one in the same condition sells for on Reverb first, because store sticker prices are a starting position, not a price.
2. Bring your own strap, picks, and a slide if you're still working on open D. A guitar that feels great sitting down with the shop's flimsy strap can feel wrong standing up for ten minutes.

**The 15-minute audition, in this order**
3. Play it unplugged first. Hold a chord and let it ring. Good wood rings and sustains; dead wood sounds like cardboard and no pickup swap fixes that. Bend a note at the 12th to 15th fret on the top three strings and listen for a fret that chokes the note out.
4. Check the neck before the finish. Run your hand up and down the fret edges, looking for sharp ends and proud frets. Sight down the edge of the neck for a twist. Ask them to show you the relief, and check the truss rod actually has room to move in both directions.
5. Play every note on every string, clean, up the whole neck. Slow and boring. This is the only way dead spots and a badly cut nut show up.
6. Check intonation at the 12th fret against the harmonic on at least the low E, G, and high E. If it's off on a brand new guitar, either it needs a setup (fine, ask them to do it) or the bridge is at its limit (walk).
7. Then plug in. Every switch position, both pickups, and roll every knob from zero to ten listening for scratch and dead spots. Wiggle the cable in the jack. Check the tuners hold after a few big bends.
8. Play it on an amp close to yours, not the $3,000 boutique thing on the floor. You're buying how it sounds in your room at your volume.

**On a Les Paul specifically**
9. Weigh it or ask. Anything over about 9.5 lb gets old at a three-hour rehearsal. Weight relief matters more than the spec sheet admits.
10. Neck profile is the real decision: 50s rounded vs 60s slim taper. Play both for five minutes each and buy the one your hand relaxes on, not the one that looks right in photos.
11. Look at the headstock and the neck heel joint for a repair line under the finish. A repaired headstock break isn't a dealbreaker on a used guitar, but it should knock 25 to 30 percent off and the seller should say it out loud.
12. Ask what pickups are in it and whether anything's been swapped. Original parts in the case is a plus, not a formality.

**Questions to put to the staff**
13. Is a setup included, and can you do it before I leave? Anything that's been sitting on a wall needs one.
14. What's the return window, in writing? Thirty days, no restocking fee, is what you want. If they won't put it in writing, that tells you something.
15. Does the case come with it, and is there a warranty card? A Les Paul without a hardshell case is a $150 hidden cost.

**The walk-away rules**
16. If it needs fretwork or a neck reset to play right, walk. There are thousands of these.
17. If you play it and immediately start mentally justifying the price, put it down and try two others. The one you come back to is the one.
18. Play at least three guitars before you commit to one, even if the first one already won. Comparison is what turns a preference into a decision.

One last thing: test a slide in open D on the shop floor. Wider string spacing and a flatter radius make slide easier, and if the store tunes down for you, check that the intonation still holds after the drop. That's a five-second check that saves a lot of frustration at home.

Kitchens don't get dirty in one big event, they get dirty in a hundred tiny re-accumulations. So the fix isn't a bigger cleaning day, it's removing the friction that makes tidying feel like a chore you postpone. Here's the system I'd run.

**1. The daily 10-minute reset (the whole game).** Once a day, ideally right after dinner, run this in order. Set a timer; it genuinely takes ten minutes if you don't detour:

- Dishes out of the sink and into the dishwasher or drying rack first. Everything else in the room depends on the sink being empty.
- Counters wiped from the back edge toward the sink, not in circles. Wipe the stovetop while it's still slightly warm, that's when grease lifts.
- Anything that doesn't live on the counter goes back where it lives, one trip only. No staging piles.
- Trash and recycling out, wipe the bin rim.
- Sink rinsed and the drain run for five seconds, then a dry cloth pass on the faucet and handle. Done.

The cue that you're finished: sink empty, counters bare, no wet cloth left balled up on the granite (leave it draped to dry or it milks the stone and smells).

**2. Create friction for clutter, not for cleaning.** You already bought the utensil holder for exactly this reason. Extend that logic: give every category of thing a single home (one drawer for towels, one for wraps, one for small appliances), and be ruthless that the counter is not storage. A countertop item only earns its spot if you use it most days. The stand mixer, the air fryer, the knife block, whatever's getting used twice a week, put it away and the surface stops reading as "mess" even when it's the same objects.

**3. Zone the clean, so a mess never spreads.** Treat the kitchen as three zones: prep/counter, sink, and cook/stove. Each has its own cleaning trigger. Stove and backsplash get a wipe after any cooking that spatters. Sink gets scrubbed (baking soda, then a splash of vinegar, scrub, rinse) once a week, because a clean-looking sink is what makes the whole room read as clean. Countertops get a proper disinfect pass daily, and the crumbs go behind and under appliances once a week.

**4. Weekly, 20 minutes, and worth a reminder.** Floors (sweep then mop), the microwave interior (bowl of water and lemon, four minutes, then wipe, steam does the work), the fridge shelf with the milk on it, and the outsides of cabinet doors around the handles, which is where grease actually collects and nobody looks. Biweekly: pull the fridge out a foot and clean behind it, run a dishwasher cleaning tablet, and degrease the range hood filter in hot water and dish soap.

**5. One thing specific to your granite.** Skip vinegar and any acidic or abrasive cleaner on the stone, it etches the seal. Warm water with a drop of dish soap, dry immediately, and reseal every six to twelve months (water bead test tells you it's due: if water soaks in instead of beading, reseal). That also keeps the scratches near the sink from getting worse.

**The failure rule.** If you find yourself doing a big two-hour clean every few weeks, that's the signal the daily reset isn't happening, not that you need a better deep-clean routine. Fix the ten minutes and the deep cleans stop being events.

Want me to turn this into a one-page printable checklist, daily on the fridge and weekly underneath? And tell me one detail that would sharpen it: do you cook most nights, and is there anyone else in the house whose stuff lands on those counters?

Most slow cooker problems trace back to two facts about the machine: it's a sealed, moist oven, so almost nothing evaporates, and its heat is low and fixed. Every rule below follows from those two, so fix these and the food gets better immediately.

1. **Liquid is the number one killer.** People pour in stock until things float, then wonder why it's soup. Use roughly 1/2 to 1 cup of liquid for most dishes. The meat and vegetables will release their own. If it looks dry at the start, it's fine, it will not be dry in four hours.
2. **Brown your meat first, and bloom your spices.** The cooker cannot create browning or Maillard flavor. Sear meat in a skillet until it's got color, and toast ground spices in that same pan for 30 seconds before they go in. This one step is most of the difference between "fine" and "good."
3. **Pick the right cut.** Tougher, fattier cuts (chuck, pork shoulder, chicken thighs) turn into something better than they started. Lean cuts (chicken breast, sirloin) turn into sawdust. The collagen is the whole point.
4. **Stop opening the lid.** Every peek drops the internal temp and adds 20 to 30 minutes. If you have a glass lid, look, don't lift.
5. **Cut for even cooking.** Uniform 1.5 to 2 inch chunks. Root vegetables go on the bottom (they need the most heat and time), meat on top.
6. **Add the fragile stuff late.** Dairy, fresh herbs, and anything you want to keep bright go in the last 15 to 30 minutes. They break or go flat if they cook for hours.
7. **"Low" is usually hotter than you think.** Older and cheaper cookers run hot on low, which is why beans scorch and vegetables turn to mush. If yours runs hot, cook on low but shorten the time, or invest in one with a real warm setting.

The honest shortcut: for weeknight cooking, steps 1 and 2 are 80 percent of your results. Nail those two and you can ignore the rest until you feel like tinkering.

For your gluten-free and plant-friendly direction, the highest-leverage upgrade is building flavor without the traditional roux or flour thickener at the end. A cornstarch slurry (1 tbsp cornstarch to 2 tbsp cold water) or a pureed can of white beans both thicken beautifully and keep it GF.

Want me to tune one specific dish you keep getting wrong (stew, chili, a bean pot, pulled pork) into an exact recipe with ratios and timing? Tell me which one and what's going off, and I'll rebuild just that one.

A small gathering is a packaging problem before it's a recipe problem. Colleagues standing around a table, holding drinks, no forks, no plates. So whatever you bake has to be grab-one and eat-one-handed. That single constraint kills half the list and makes the decision easy.

Here's the short menu, pick one or two:

Brown the butter first (melt, keep cooking until the milk solids go nut-brown and smell like toffee) then let it cool before it hits the eggs. 170g butter, 200g brown sugar, 1 egg + 1 yolk, 200g flour, pinch salt, 150g chopped chocolate or walnuts. Bake 350°F / 175°C for 22-25 min, pull while the center is still just barely underdone.

**2. Chewy chocolate chip cookies.** You already ran these for an event, so you know the drill. They're the universal crowd-pleaser and they stack and travel. **3. Mini lemon poppyseed loaves.** You nailed the lemon poppyseed cake for the going-away party, so this is the same batter in a different vehicle. **4. A savory anchor, if you want balance.** Cheddar-chive scones or a baked savory galette cut into wedges. When you've got coffee and a pile of sweet things, one savory item gets demolished first.

One practical note regardless of which you pick: bake the day before, cool completely, then store airtight. Cookies and blondies keep 3-4 days room temp, mini loaves 2-3 days room temp or a week in the fridge. Don't refrigerate the cookies, they go stale faster in the cold.
